PSI COMP80 · the 3 KB ROM · 0000–0BFF

COMP80 ROM Listings

Annotated listings of the PSI COMP80's ROMs: the monitor that every ROM starts with (as made in 1979, or in a key-safe version that a key cannot restart), and the twenty-one languages and programs that can sit above it in the remaining 2 KB. BURP is the original, from the Wireless World articles; FORTH, LISP, BASIC, Logo, CHIP-8, FOCAL, PILOT, ZASM, Prolog, VTL-2, Mouse, Befunge, CALC, TRAC, PL/0, BF, ED, FILE, QUEST and APL were written for this project. Every line shows its address and the bytes it assembles to, read from the ROM images, and every name or branch address is a link to the line it means.

See also the screenshots, the LISP page, the hardware and the emulator, which runs all twenty-one ROMs.

0000–03FFMonitor ROM, 1 KB
0400–0BFFBURP or another language, 2 KB
0C00–1FFFRAM, 5 KB
8000–87FFScreen, 64 × 32
MonitorKey-safeBURPFORTHLISPBASICLogoCHIP-8FOCALPILOTZASMPrologVTL-2MouseBefungeCALCTRACPL/0BFEDFILEQUESTAPLHex dumps
0000–03FF

Monitor

The first kilobyte of every COMP80 ROM, the same in all three. Reset clears the screen and prints READY. Keys arrive as non-maskable interrupts: the handler at 0066 echoes each key on the screen, and a command key turns into a jump to its command. The commands examine, change, move, fill, find and list memory, read and write tape, and run code; RS (the ^ key) enters the language at 0800.

An annotated disassembly. The names and comments come from the earlier disassemblies (now in old/), corrected where the bytes disagreed. Source: rom/psicomp80.asm, assembled after rom/monitor_original.asm; the lines of the key-safe monitor have no bytes here.

PSI COMP80 Monitor (first 1KB of ROM) - annotated disassembly                   ; ORG 0000h (monitor mapped at 0x0000 at reset)                   ;                   ; Keyboard notes:                   ;   IN A,($01) reads the latched key byte (active-low), then CPL inverts it.                   ;   CP A,1Eh / JP Z,0800h implements the RS key (ASCII 0x1E, Record Separator) to enter BURP.                   ;                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------                   ; Key/Control-code conventions observed in this monitor ROM                   ;                   ; The keyboard hardware delivers an active-low keycode on port $01.                   ; The monitor inverts it (CPL) and then normalises certain values:                   ;   - 0x0D (CR/ENTER) is remapped to 0x1F (US) as the monitor’s                   ;     internal end-of-line marker.                   ;   - For codes >= 0x40, the monitor ANDs with 0x1F, effectively                   ;     folding uppercase letters to 1..26 (A=1, B=2, ... Z=26).                   ;     This means command keywords like ALPH/LIST/etc are NOT stored                   ;     as ASCII strings in ROM; they’re matched using these 5-bit codes.                   ;                   ; Control characters used as special keys:                   ;   0x1C  FS  (File Separator)  - acts as an escape back to command state                   ;         (Monitor docs mention: in ALT mode, type FS to return to commands).                   ;   0x1D  GS  (Group Separator) - used as a delimiter/terminator in some input loops.                   ;   0x1E  RS  (Record Separator)- ‘RS’ key to enter BURP (JP 0800h).                   ;   0x1F  US  (Unit Separator)  - used internally as ‘end of line’ (remapped from CR).                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; Monitor command dispatch (as observed in ROM)                   ; The monitor reads a normalised command selector in A from CALL $0355 and                   ; compares it against a small set of command IDs, then jumps to handlers.                   ; These IDs are *not* ASCII; they are compact key/command codes produced by                   ; the monitor's command scanner.                   ;                   ; Mappings below are inferred from the handler behaviour and monitor_cmds.md:                   ;   $FC : RUN  XXXX     (parse address -> JP (HL))        ()                   ;   $13 : ALT           (alter memory; loops until FS/RESET)                   ;   $0F : COR           (scan/replace AA->BB across range)                   ;   $FE : FIND          (search for consecutive bytes XX YY)                   ;   $08 : LIST          (list memory to screen)                   ;   $04 : PRINT         (list memory on second output device)                   ;   $F1 : TAPE          (write block to tape/serial on port $20)                   ;   $F2 : READ          (read tape into memory via port $00)                   ;   $07 : ALPH          (VDU alphanumeric test pattern)                   ;   $FD : PROM          (program $1C00-$1CFF via ports)  ()                   ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; === v5: relabelled command dispatch + monitor commands ===                    CMD_RUN_CODE:   EQU $FC                   CMD_LOAD_CODE:  EQU $F8                   CMD_MOV_CODE:   EQU $09                   CMD_FILL_CODE:  EQU $06                   CMD_PROM_CODE:  EQU $FD                   CMD_ALT_CODE:   EQU $13                   CMD_COR_CODE:   EQU $0F                   CMD_FIND_CODE:  EQU $FE                   CMD_LIST_CODE:  EQU $08                   CMD_PRINT_CODE: EQU $04                   CMD_TAPE_CODE:  EQU $F1                   CMD_READ_CODE:  EQU $F2                   CMD_ALPH_CODE:  EQU $07                            ORG     $0000 0000               MON_START:0000  31 DF 1F             LD SP,$1FDF           0003  11 00 80             LD DE,$8000           0006  CD CE 03             CALL PRINT_INLINE     ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; NMI (keyboard 'data ready') handler at 0066h                   ;                   ; Key idea: the COMP-80 generates an NMI on any keyboard event. The monitor *expects*                   ; this NMI to occur only while it is deliberately waiting in a HALT instruction.                   ;                   ; On NMI entry, the Z80 pushes the return address (PC) to the stack. This handler                   ; swaps that return address into HL (EX (SP),HL), backs up one byte, and checks the                   ; opcode that was interrupted. If it wasn't HALT (0x76), it treats this as an                   ; unexpected key interrupt and resets back to 0000h.                   ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                    if KEYSAFE                   ; The key-safe monitor (rom/monitor_keysafe.asm): a key that comes while the                   ; CPU is not in a HALT is ignored, and the program carries on with all its                   ; registers, instead of the monitor being restarted (the key is read and                   ; dropped).  PUSH AF keeps the                   ; program's A and flags until the HALT is checked for; the stack is back as                   ; it was before the key is read, so programs that keep SP in ROM (Storm, the                   ; memory dump) see the same handler. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; $0355: GETKEY/GETCMD – wait for a keypress using HALT+NMI, then decode it                   ;                   ; The COMP-80 monitor uses the Z80 NMI (vector $0066) as its keyboard interrupt.                   ; The mainline executes HALT to sleep until an NMI arrives. The NMI handler:                   ;   * verifies the CPU really was halted (checks the interrupted opcode == $76)                   ;     and jumps to $0000 (cold monitor restart) if not halted                   ;   * reads the keyboard latch via IN A,($01) / CPL and normalises the value                   ;     (letters folded to 1..26 via AND $1F, CR remapped, etc.)                   ;   * returns with RETN, leaving the decoded key value in A                   ;                   ; This routine ($0355) then performs a small decode/debounce sequence:                   ;   1) Sample 1: HALT -> A, take low 5 bits (A AND $1F) into B                   ;   2) Writes that sample to $8010 (scratch/display state)                   ;   3) Sample 2: HALT -> A, take low 5 bits into C                   ;   4) Waits until the key returns to idle (A == $20, SPACE) before completing                   ;   5) Returns A = (C - B).  This appears to be the monitor's compact keycode                   ;      decode step (two successive samples combined via subtraction).                   ;                   ; NOTE: The exact meaning of B and C depends on the keyboard encoder; empirically                   ; the final A is the command selector used by the dispatch compares near $0080.                   ; --------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0355               GET_KEY_SELECTOR:0355  C5                   PUSH BC               0356  76                   HALT                  0357  E6 1F                AND $1F               0359  47                   LD B,A                035A  11 01 80             LD DE,$8001           035D  CD C4 03             CALL PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE ; ------------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE_64COL  (entry at 03C4)                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ; This effectively advances to the                   ;   start of the next screen line on the COMP-80 (64 chars/row).                   ;                   ; How it works:                   ;   - Uses RST 20h to output a SPACE at (DE) and increment DE.                   ;   - Loops until (E & 0x3F) == 0, then exits via the common epilogue at 03DB.                   ;   - Prologue EX (SP),HL preserves caller HL using the same stack trick as the                   ;     inline string printer at 03CE (shared epilogue).                   ;03C4               PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE:03C4  E3                   EX (SP),HL            ; preserve caller HL via return-address swap (shared epilogue pattern)03C5  F5                   PUSH AF               ; save AF (A used for column check / clobbered by output)03C6               L03C6:03C6  7B                   LD A,E                ; A = current column (low byte of cursor)03C7  E6 3F                AND $3F               ; mask to 0..63 (column within 64-char row)03C9  28 10                JR Z,L03DB            ; if already at col 0, exit via epilogue at 03DB03CB  E7                   RST $20               ; output SPACE at (DE), increment DE (see RST 20h)03CC  18 F8                JR L03C6              ; loop until aligned                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; STR_PRINT_INLINE_AT_RETADDR  (entry at 03CE)                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ;   Print an inline, terminator-delimited string placed immediately after the CALL                   ;   instruction. (GS = 1Dh)03D4  28 05                JR Z,L03DB            ; yes -> finish (return address now points past terminator)03D6  CD 82 00             CALL L0082            ; output this character03D9  18 F5                JR L03D0              ; loop for next byte03DB               L03DB:03DB  F1                   POP AF                ; restore A03DC  E3                   EX (SP),HL            ; put updated HL back as return address; restore original HL03DD  C9                   RET                   ; returns to byte after terminator in caller stream                   ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; HEX INPUT HELPERS                   ;                   ; 03DE  HEXWORD(): read 4 hex digits from the keyboard and return the 16-bit                   ;       value in HL (high byte first). 0383  LIST_PAD_TO_START_BYTE_COLUMN                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ;   When a LIST-style dump begins at an address not aligned to a 16-byte                   ;   boundary, this routine outputs the correct number of SPACE characters so                   ;   that the *first printed data byte* appears under the proper column.                   ;                   ; Operation (conceptual):                   ;   i = L & 0x0F          ; byte index within a 16-byte line                   ;   spaces =                   ;       3*i               ; 'HH ' per byte (two hex chars + space)                   ;     + 2*(i/4)           ; extra group spacing every 4 bytes                   ;                   ;   Outputs that many spaces using RST 20h, advancing DE accordingly.                   ;                   ; Why this exists:                   ;   LIST output groups bytes in sets of four with extra spacing. If LIST                   ;   starts at (say) xxxx3, the address header is printed first, then this                   ;   routine pads so the first byte printed lines up under the correct column.                   ;                   ; Call sites (from v15):                   ;   - 00A6 : align listing output before printing first data byte                   ;   - 0326 : LIST command, align for unaligned start address                   ;                   ; =============================================================================
0000–03FF

Key-safe monitor

The monitor with one change, made for this project. The original handler at 0066 restarts the monitor when a key comes while the CPU is not waiting in a HALT, so a key stops a running program; this one ignores such a key and the program carries on with all its registers. It needs ten more bytes, so the code from 0095 to 012F moves up by ten into the free bytes that were at 0130. Every entry point a language uses (03xx) is where it was, and each language ROM also comes with this monitor, as psicomp80_<lang>_ks.rom; BURP's one call into the moved code is assembled to match. Source: rom/psicomp80.asm, assembled after rom/monitor_keysafe.asm.

  IN A,($01) reads the latched key byte (active-low), then CPL inverts it.                   ;   CP A,1Eh / JP Z,0800h implements the RS key (ASCII 0x1E, Record Separator) to enter BURP.                   ;                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------                   ; Key/Control-code conventions observed in this monitor ROM                   ;                   ; The keyboard hardware delivers an active-low keycode on port $01.                   ; The monitor inverts it (CPL) and then normalises certain values:                   ;   - 0x0D (CR/ENTER) is remapped to 0x1F (US) as the monitor’s                   ;     internal end-of-line marker.                   ;   - For codes >= 0x40, the monitor ANDs with 0x1F, effectively                   ;     folding uppercase letters to 1..26 (A=1, B=2, ... Z=26).                   ;     This means command keywords like ALPH/LIST/etc are NOT stored                   ;     as ASCII strings in ROM; they’re matched using these 5-bit codes.                   ;                   ; Control characters used as special keys:                   ;   0x1C  FS  (File Separator)  - acts as an escape back to command state                   ;         (Monitor docs mention: in ALT mode, type FS to return to commands).                   ;   0x1D  GS  (Group Separator) - used as a delimiter/terminator in some input loops.                   ;   0x1E  RS  (Record Separator)- ‘RS’ key to enter BURP (JP 0800h).                   ;   0x1F  US  (Unit Separator)  - used internally as ‘end of line’ (remapped from CR).                   ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; $0355: GETKEY/GETCMD – wait for a keypress using HALT+NMI, then decode it                   ;                   ; The COMP-80 monitor uses the Z80 NMI (vector $0066) as its keyboard interrupt.                   ; The mainline executes HALT to sleep until an NMI arrives. The NMI handler:                   ;   * verifies the CPU really was halted (checks the interrupted opcode == $76)                   ;     and jumps to $0000 (cold monitor restart) if not halted                   ;   * reads the keyboard latch via IN A,($01) / CPL and normalises the value                   ;     (letters folded to 1..26 via AND $1F, CR remapped, etc.)                   ;   * returns with RETN, leaving the decoded key value in A                   ;                   ; This routine ($0355) then performs a small decode/debounce sequence:                   ;   1) Sample 1: HALT -> A, take low 5 bits (A AND $1F) into B                   ;   2) Writes that sample to $8010 (scratch/display state)                   ;   3) Sample 2: HALT -> A, take low 5 bits into C                   ;   4) Waits until the key returns to idle (A == $20, SPACE) before completing                   ;   5) Returns A = (C - B).  This appears to be the monitor's compact keycode                   ;      decode step (two successive samples combined via subtraction).                   ;                   ; NOTE: The exact meaning of B and C depends on the keyboard encoder; empirically                   ; the final A is the command selector used by the dispatch compares near $0080.                   ; --------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0355               GET_KEY_SELECTOR:0355  C5                   PUSH BC               0356  76                   HALT                  0357  E6 1F                AND $1F               0359  47                   LD B,A                035A  11 01 80             LD DE,$8001           035D  CD C4 03             CALL PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE ; ------------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE_64COL  (entry at 03C4)                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ; This effectively advances to the                   ;   start of the next screen line on the COMP-80 (64 chars/row).                   ;                   ; How it works:                   ;   - Uses RST 20h to output a SPACE at (DE) and increment DE.                   ;   - Loops until (E & 0x3F) == 0, then exits via the common epilogue at 03DB.                   ;   - Prologue EX (SP),HL preserves caller HL using the same stack trick as the                   ;     inline string printer at 03CE (shared epilogue).                   ;03C4               PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE:03C4  E3                   EX (SP),HL            ; preserve caller HL via return-address swap (shared epilogue pattern)03C5  F5                   PUSH AF               ; save AF (A used for column check / clobbered by output)03C6               L03C6:03C6  7B                   LD A,E                ; A = current column (low byte of cursor)03C7  E6 3F                AND $3F               ; mask to 0..63 (column within 64-char row)03C9  28 10                JR Z,L03DB            ; if already at col 0, exit via epilogue at 03DB03CB  E7                   RST $20               ; output SPACE at (DE), increment DE (see RST 20h)03CC  18 F8                JR L03C6              ; loop until aligned                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; STR_PRINT_INLINE_AT_RETADDR  (entry at 03CE)                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ;   Print an inline, terminator-delimited string placed immediately after the CALL                   ;   instruction. This is how the monitor prints the READY prompt at reset.                   ;                   ; Calling convention (Z80 trick):                   ;   Caller does:   CALL 03CE                   ;                 DB <byte0>,<byte1>,...,<terminator>                   ;   On entry, the return address (address of the first DB byte) is on the stack.                   ;   EX (SP),HL swaps that return address into HL, giving HL = string pointer.                   ;   When printing finishes, EX (SP),HL puts the *updated* HL back on the stack,                   ;   so RET returns to the byte *after* the terminator.                   ;                   ; String format:                   ;   Bytes are COMP-80 keyboard/display codes (often 5-bit letters: A=01..Z=1A,                   ;   plus space=20h). Terminator is GS = 1Dh.                   ;                   ; Output:                   ;   Each byte is sent to the normal character output routine at 0082.                   ; ------------------------------------------------------------------------------03CE               PRINT_INLINE:03CE  E3                   EX (SP),HL            ; HL <- return address (string ptr), [SP] <- old HL03CF  F5                   PUSH AF               ; preserve A across printing03D0               L03D0:03D0  7E                   LD A,(HL)             ; fetch next byte of inline string03D1  23                   INC HL                ; advance pointer03D2  FE 1D                CP $1D                ; terminator? (GS = 1Dh)03D4  28 05                JR Z,L03DB            ; yes -> finish (return address now points past terminator)03D6  CD 82 00             CALL L0082            ; output this character03D9  18 F5                JR L03D0              ; loop for next byte03DB               L03DB:03DB  F1                   POP AF                ; restore A03DC  E3                   EX (SP),HL            ; put updated HL back as return address; restore original HL03DD  C9                   RET                   ; returns to byte after terminator in caller stream                   ; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------                   ; HEX INPUT HELPERS                   ;                   ; 03DE  HEXWORD(): read 4 hex digits from the keyboard and return the 16-bit                   ;       value in HL (high byte first). 0383  LIST_PAD_TO_START_BYTE_COLUMN                   ;                   ; Purpose:                   ;   When a LIST-style dump begins at an address not aligned to a 16-byte                   ;   boundary, this routine outputs the correct number of SPACE characters so                   ;   that the *first printed data byte* appears under the proper column.                   ;                   ; Operation (conceptual):                   ;   i = L & 0x0F          ; byte index within a 16-byte line                   ;   spaces =                   ;       3*i               ; 'HH ' per byte (two hex chars + space)                   ;     + 2*(i/4)           ; extra group spacing every 4 bytes                   ;                   ;   Outputs that many spaces using RST 20h, advancing DE accordingly.                   ;                   ; Why this exists:                   ;   LIST output groups bytes in sets of four with extra spacing. If LIST                   ;   starts at (say) xxxx3, the address header is printed first, then this                   ;   routine pads so the first byte printed lines up under the correct column.                   ;                   ; Call sites (from v15):                   ;   - 00A6 : align listing output before printing first data byte                   ;   - 0326 : LIST command, align for unaligned start address                   ;                   ; =============================================================================
0400–0BFF

BURP

The language in the original ROM, from the Wireless World articles: a small BASIC-like language whose arithmetic is done by a National MM57109 calculator chip. The Z80 sends the chip its key codes (MM_SEND) and reads back the digits of the result (MM_OUT_X). Entry is BURP_ENTRY; from 0BB5 the ROM holds the articles' sample program.

An annotated disassembly, in the same file as the monitor: rom/psicomp80.asm.

The 4 digit out lines are blanked odd so that                   ;  only the READY and BR lines both initally high get through (0591). By continually reading                   ;  and jumping back on even parity the Z80 is effectively waiting for one of these two lines to become active.                   ;  If it is the BR line the Z80 outputs a NOP to the 57109 (because when tests prove true the 57109                   ; Low nibble selects which 16-byte block.                   ;         Bit4 selects base page: 0 -> $1E00, 1 -> $1F00.                   ;    OUT: HL = base + (A & $0F) * 16, where base is $1E00 or $1F00.                   ;    Flags: C is used as a convenient bit4 test (carry after 4x RLA).                   ;                   ;  Implementation notes:                   ;    AND A clears carry. Four RLA operations effectively compute (A << 4)                   ;    and leave carry = original bit4. L receives the shifted value.                   ;    If carry set (original bit4=1) H is incremented to select page $1Fxx.                   ;                    ; COMP80 FORTH                   ;                   ; A small FORTH for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that                   ; held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS                   ; key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Direct-threaded code.  Registers while FORTH runs:                   ;   BC = top of data stack       DE = instruction pointer (IP)                   ;   SP = rest of data stack      IX = return stack pointer                   ;   IY = NEXT (every primitive ends with JP (IY))       HL, A = scratch                   ;                   ; Text is kept in ASCII (20h-5Fh) and converted to the display's 6-bit codes                   ; on output.  The keyboard folds letters to 01h-1Ah; RAWKEY turns them back.                   ;                   ; Keys.  The monitor's NMI handler echoes each key at (DE) and folds codes                   ; 40h and up to 5 bits, so Backspace (08h) and H come out the same.  RS (the ^                   ; key) makes it jump to 0800h; if that happens while FORTH waits in RAWKEY                   ; (the return address on the stack is KEYRET), ENTRY treats it as rubout                   ; instead of a restart.  FS (Ctrl+\) goes back to the monitor.  Any key while                   ; a program runs makes the NMI handler reset to the monitor; RS then comes                   ; back to FORTH with the dictionary kept.                   ;                   ; Screen: line 0 shows FORTH (where the monitor shows READY); lines 1-31                   ; scroll.                   ;                   ; Dictionary header: link (2), length + 80h if immediate (1), name, code.                   ; The user dictionary starts at 0C00h, so TAPE 0C00 <HERE> saves it along                   ; with the three variables in front of it.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the dictionary below is valid                   LATEST: equ 0C02h           ; newest header                   DP:     equ 0C04h           ; HERE                   DICT0:  equ 0C06h           ; first free byte of a new dictionary                   MAGICV: equ 0F04Dh                    TIB:    equ 1D00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   WBUF:   equ 1D50h           ; parsed word, counted (80 bytes)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   BASE:   equ 1DA2h                   STATE:  equ 1DA4h           ; byte: 0 interpreting, 1 compiling                   TOIN:   equ 1DA6h           ; byte: parse offset into TIB                   NTIB:   equ 1DA7h           ; byte: characters in TIB                   LASTH:  equ 1DA8h           ; newest header made by mkhdr                   R0:     equ 1E40h           ; return stack grows down from here                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; data stack grows down from here (monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ;                    ; COMP80 LISP                   ;                   ; A small LISP for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that                   ; held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS                   ; key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Objects are 16-bit words:                   ;   NIL          0                   ;   number n     2n+1 (odd), so -16384..16383                   ;   built-in     2k for built-in function k (below 100h)                   ;   symbol       address of its record in 0C20h-0EFFh: value (2), length                   ;                (1), name; records start on even addresses                   ;   cell         address of a 4-byte cell, car then cdr, in the heap                   ;                (1000h up, or 8800h up with the 32 KB expansion)                   ; so anything from 1000h up that is even is a cell.                   ;                   ; Variables are dynamically scoped with shallow binding: a symbol's value is                   ; in its record, and calling a LAMBDA saves the old values of its parameters                   ; on the binding stack and puts them back when it returns, or when an error                   ; unwinds.  The binding stack grows up from the end of the mark bitmap                   ; (BMEND) and the Z80 stack down from STOP towards it.                   ;                   ; Garbage collection is mark and sweep, with a mark bitmap.  The roots are                   ; the symbol table, the binding stack and the Z80 stack, which is scanned                   ; conservatively: any word on it that could be a cell is taken as one.  So                   ; code only has to keep what it still needs on the stack when it conses.                   ; Free cells have UNB in their car and are chained through their cdr.                   ;                   ; Text is kept in ASCII (20h-5Fh) and converted to the display's 6-bit codes                   ; on output.  Keys and the screen work as in COMP80 FORTH (forth/forth.asm):                   ; RS while waiting for a key is rubout, any key while a program runs resets                   ; to the monitor, and RS from there comes back to LISP with everything kept.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the RAM below holds a LISP world                   SYMEND: equ 0C02h           ; end of the symbol table                   FREE:   equ 0C04h           ; free list                   HEAP:   equ 0C06h           ; first cell        } set at cold start                   HSIZE:  equ 0C08h           ; heap size, bytes  } from MEM16 or MEM48                   BMAP:   equ 0C0Ah           ; mark bitmap       }                   BMEND:  equ 0C0Ch           ; end of the bitmap }                   BSP:    equ 0C0Eh           ; binding stack pointer                   NFREE:  equ 0C10h           ; free cells after the last collection                   CURS:   equ 0C12h           ; output position in screen memory                   TOIN:   equ 0C14h           ; byte: read offset into TIB                   NTIB:   equ 0C15h           ; byte: characters in TIB                   SYMS:   equ 0C20h           ; symbol table, up to SYMTOP                   SYMTOP: equ 0F00h                   TIB:    equ 0F00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   WBUF:   equ 0F50h           ; atom being read, counted                   STOP:   equ 1F00h           ; Z80 stack grows down from here (monitor uses 1Fxx)                   MARGIN: equ 80              ; room kept between the two stacks                   MAGICV: equ 0D15Ah                   UNB:    equ 0FEh            ; value of an unbound symbol; car of a free cell                    NILSYM: equ SYMS            ; the first four symbol records (see NAMES)                   TSYM:   equ SYMS+6                   QUOSYM: equ SYMS+10                   LAMSYM: equ SYMS+18                   FSLIM:  equ 18              ; built-ins below this are special forms                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- cells                    ; HL = car or cdr of HL; NIL gives NIL.                    ; COMP80 BASIC                   ;                   ; A Tiny BASIC for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that                   ; held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS                   ; key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Integer BASIC: 16-bit signed numbers, variables A-Z and an array @(I),                   ; numbered program lines kept as typed, statements PRINT INPUT LET IF GOTO                   ; GOSUB RETURN FOR NEXT REM END RUN LIST NEW, and graphics: PLOT and UNPLOT                   ; on the 128 x 62 quarter-character points of lines 1-31, POINT(X,Y) to test                   ; one, and CLS.                   ;                   ; The program is kept as typed, each line its number (2 bytes, low first),                   ; its text without the leading spaces, and 0Dh.  Lines are in order from                   ; 0C04h up to TXTEND, and @() is in the free space after them.  Statements                   ; are run straight from the text: DE is the text pointer throughout.                   ;                   ; FOR and GOSUB keep frames on the Z80 stack, which is otherwise empty                   ; between statements.  A GOSUB frame is the text pointer, the line and a 0                   ; on top; a FOR frame is the step, the limit, the text pointer, the line                   ; and the variable's address on top.  A 0FFFFh at the bottom marks the end.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are handled as in COMP80 FORTH: the monitor's NMI handler                   ; echoes each key and wakes the HALT in RAWKEY; RS while waiting is a rubout                   ; and RS at any other time (re)starts BASIC, keeping the program.  Any key                   ; while a program runs resets to the monitor; RS comes back with the                   ; program kept.  Line 0 shows BASIC; lines 1-31 scroll.                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the program below is valid                   TXTEND: equ 0C02h           ; end of the program                   PROG:   equ 0C04h           ; first line                   MAGICV: equ 0BA5Ch                   TOPH:   equ 1Ch             ; the program and @() end below 1C00h                   VARS:   equ 1C00h           ; A-Z at 1C02h-1C35h                   TIB:    equ 1D00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   CURLN:  equ 1DA2h           ; the line running, 0 for a line typed in                   RNDV:   equ 1DA4h           ; random number                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; stack (monitor uses 1Fxx)                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- tables                   ; Each entry is a name with 80h added to its last letter, then the address                   ; to go to.                    ; COMP80 LOGO                   ;                   ; A small Logo for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that                   ; held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS                   ; key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Screen: line 0 shows LOGO (where the monitor shows READY).  Lines 1-26 are                   ; the turtle's field: 128 x 52 quarter-character points.  Lines 27-31 are                   ; for typing and printing, and scroll on their own.                   ;                   ; The turtle.  A quarter character is 3 units wide and 5 tall on the screen,                   ; so a turtle step is one point across but 0.6 of a point up or down, and a                   ; square comes out square.  The field is 128 steps across and 86 up.  X and                   ; Y are kept in points with 8 bits of fraction, with HOME (0,0) in the                   ; middle; the heading is in degrees, 0 up and clockwise.  FD draws a point                   ; at every step.                   ;                   ; The interpreter works on the text itself.  A line, or a procedure's body,                   ; is a run of words: numbers, :NAMES (variables), "NAMES (quoted words),                   ; and the single characters [ ] ( ) + - * / < = >.  A - after a space and                   ; before a digit starts a negative number instead, so SETXY 0 -40 is two                   ; numbers, as in other Logos.  A ; ends the line.                   ; Numbers are 16-bit signed integers.                   ;                   ; Procedures (TO ... END) are kept as text: link (2 bytes), then the words                   ; from the name to the word before END, one space apart, and a 0.                   ; Variables are a table of name pointer (2) + value (2): MAKE's globals grow                   ; down from VB, a procedure's inputs are pushed above VB as it is called and                   ; dropped when it returns.  A name is looked up from the newest entry down,                   ; so scope is dynamic, as in other Logos.                   ;                   ; Keys.  The monitor's NMI handler echoes each key at (DE) and folds codes                   ; 40h and up to 5 bits.  RS (the ^ key) makes it jump to 0800h; if that                   ; happens while LOGO waits in RAWKEY, ENTRY treats it as rubout.  FS                   ; (Ctrl+\) goes back to the monitor.  Any key while a program runs makes the                   ; NMI handler reset to the monitor; RS then comes back to LOGO with the                   ; procedures kept.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the procedures below are valid                   LATEST: equ 0C02h           ; newest procedure                   HERE:   equ 0C04h           ; first free byte                   GP:     equ 0C06h           ; lowest global variable                   PROC0:  equ 0C08h           ; procedures start here                   MAGICV: equ 4C47h                    VB:     equ 1700h           ; globals below, procedure inputs above                   VTOP:   equ 1A00h           ; inputs stop here                    TIB:    equ 1A00h           ; input line (80 bytes and a 0)                   CURS:   equ 1A60h           ; output position in screen memory                   TPV:    equ 1A62h           ; the word being read                   BP:     equ 1A64h           ; top of the variable table                   FRAME:  equ 1A66h           ; stack of the innermost procedure, or 0                   RES:    equ 1A68h           ; OUTPUT's value                   XP:     equ 1A6Ah           ; turtle x, points * 256                   YP:     equ 1A6Ch           ; turtle y, points * 256                   HEAD:   equ 1A6Eh           ; heading, 0-359                   DX:     equ 1A70h           ; one step                   DY:     equ 1A72h                   SEED:   equ 1A74h                   PEN:    equ 1A76h           ; byte: 0 up, 1 down, 2 erase                   DLY:    equ 1A77h           ; byte: delay at each step                   STKLIM: equ 1AC0h           ; deepest the stack may go                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; stack (the monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   TXT0:   equ VRAM+27*64      ; first text line                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; CHIP-8

A CHIP-8 interpreter: the 64 × 32 CHIP-8 display is the COMP80's screen, a character a pixel. Every instruction can be restarted, so a key can come at any moment. Source: chip8/chip8.asm.

                   ; COMP80 CHIP-8                   ;                   ; A CHIP-8 interpreter for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh)                   ; that held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the                   ; RS key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h, which starts                   ; the CHIP-8 program at 0E00h from the beginning.                   ;                   ; The CHIP-8 display is 64 x 32 pixels, the size of the COMP80 screen, so                   ; each pixel is a character: a solid block (4Fh) or a space (20h).  CHIP-8                   ; memory is 4 KB, 0C00h-1BFFh: CHIP-8 address a is 0C00h + a, so programs,                   ; which start at 200h, load at 0E00h.  The hex font is copied to 0C00h.                   ;                   ; Keys while a program runs                   ; -------------------------                   ; A key strobes NMI, and the monitor's NMI handler (0066h) goes back to the                   ; monitor unless the byte before the interrupted address is a HALT (76h).                   ; As in life/life.asm, the interpreter runs with SP pointing into this ROM,                   ; at TRAP+2: the NMI's push is lost and the handler takes the ROM word at                   ; TRAP (KEYH, with a HALT byte in front of it) as the address it                   ; interrupted, so it returns to KEYH with A = the key.  Return goes through                   ; PAD_TO_NEXT_LINE (03C4h), whose CALL, RST 20h and RET use the ROM words                   ; below TRAP: 03CCh keeps it in its loop and KEYCR is where it returns.                   ;                   ; What was interrupted can't be carried on (HL, A and the flags are lost),                   ; so every CHIP-8 instruction can be started again.  The CHIP-8 registers                   ; are kept twice, in STA and STB.  An instruction copies the current set to                   ; the other, works on the copy and makes it current with a single store to                   ; CUR; a key before that store loses only the copy, and KEYH starts the                   ; instruction again.  The other writes are ones that can be done twice:                   ; memory written from registers (FX33, FX55), the return stack, CLS.  DRW                   ; first works out the new value of each character it changes into TBUF;                   ; then PEND marks TBUF ready, and the characters are written and the                   ; registers made current, which RESUME does again if a key gets in first.                   ;                   ; With SP in ROM there is no CALL, PUSH or POP while a program runs, and DE                   ; points either at SCRATCH (the NMI handler stores the key at (DE)) or into                   ; the register copy being worked on, where a stray byte does no harm.                   ;                   ; Keys: the CHIP-8 keypad    1 2 3 C   is   1 2 3 4                   ;                            4 5 6 D        Q W E R                   ;                            7 8 9 E        A S D F                   ;                            A 0 B F        Z X C V                   ; The COMP80 keyboard says when a key goes down but not when it comes up,                   ; so a key counts as held for HOLD ticks after it was pressed (a held key                   ; repeats on the host).  RS starts the program again; FS goes back to the                   ; monitor.                   ;                   ; Timing: there is no clock to read, so the interpreter waits SPEED loops                   ; before each instruction, and the 60 Hz timers count down every IPT                   ; instructions.  SPEED (1C00h) can be changed with the monitor.                    MEM:    equ 0C00h           ; CHIP-8 address 000h                   PROG:   equ 0E00h           ; CHIP-8 address 200h                    SPEED:  equ 1C00h           ; delay before each instruction                   MAGIC:  equ 1C01h           ; MAGICV once SPEED has been set                   CUR:    equ 1C02h           ; current register set (STA or STB)                   PEND:   equ 1C04h           ; register set to make current after TBUF, or 0                   NEWP:   equ 1C06h           ; register set being worked on                   ICOUNT: equ 1C08h           ; instructions left until the next tick                   TICK:   equ 1C09h           ; counts ticks                   LASTKEY: equ 1C0Ah          ; CHIP-8 key held, or 0FFh                   KEYTIME: equ 1C0Bh          ; TICK when it was pressed                   KEYSEQ: equ 1C0Ch           ; counts key presses                   SEED:   equ 1C0Eh           ; random number state                   TCOUNT: equ 1C10h           ; entries in TBUF                   COLL:   equ 1C11h           ; DRW: a pixel was turned off                   DX:     equ 1C12h           ; DRW: left column                   DY:     equ 1C13h           ; DRW: row being drawn                   NROWS:  equ 1C14h           ; DRW: rows left                   SPR:    equ 1C16h           ; DRW: next sprite byte                   COLX:   equ 1C18h           ; DRW: column being drawn                   JMPV:   equ 1C1Ah           ; jump address for DISP                   TMPW:   equ 1C1Ch                   STK:    equ 1C40h           ; CHIP-8 return stack, 16 words                   STA:    equ 1D00h           ; the two register sets, each in a block of 64                   STB:    equ 1D40h                   STHI:   equ 1Dh                    ; COMP80 FOCAL                   ;                   ; FOCAL, DEC's 1968 interactive language, for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB                   ; of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is                   ; unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler                   ; jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Numbers are floating point, 8 digits, done by the MM57109 calculator chip                   ; as in BURP.  An expression is worked out by sending it to the chip as it                   ; is parsed: each number or variable is keyed into the chip, which pushes                   ; its stack, and each operator is sent after its right-hand side.  The chip                   ; stack holds four numbers, so an expression can have at most four values                   ; waiting at once (2+3*(4-5/6) is fine; deeper nesting loses the oldest).                   ; A variable keeps the 12 digits the chip's OUT instruction gives (exponent,                   ; signs, mantissa) and is keyed back in digit by digit.                   ;                   ; Commands are known by their first letter, as in FOCAL:                   ;   TYPE  ASK  SET  IF  GOTO  DO  RETURN  FOR  COMMENT  QUIT  WRITE  ERASE                   ; Functions: FSQT FABS FSIN FCOS FATN FEXP FLOG FITR FRAN.                   ;                   ; A program line is stored as its number (step, group: so the word is                   ; group*256 + step) followed by its text and a 0.  Lines go up from PROG;                   ; variables (2 bytes of name, 12 of digits) go down from VTOP.                   ;                   ; Keys.  As in FORTH: RS while waiting for a key is rubout; any key while a                   ; program runs makes the monitor's NMI handler reset to the monitor, and RS                   ; then comes back to FOCAL with the program kept.  FS goes to the monitor.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the program below is valid                   PEND:   equ 0C02h           ; end of the program                   VBOT:   equ 0C04h           ; lowest variable                   SEED:   equ 0C06h           ; FRAN                   CURS:   equ 0C08h           ; output position in screen memory                   CUR:    equ 0C0Ah           ; line running (0 in direct mode)                   JUMP:   equ 0C0Ch           ; line to go to                   FLOW:   equ 0C0Eh           ; byte: 0 go on, 1 GOTO (JUMP), 2 RETURN                   ASKF:   equ 0C0Fh           ; byte: 1 in ASK, 0 in TYPE                   FV:     equ 0C10h           ; the FOR running: its variable,                   FS:     equ 0C12h           ; the text of its step (0: 1),                   FE:     equ 0C14h           ; of its end,                   FB:     equ 0C16h           ; and of the rest of the line                   PROG:   equ 0C18h                   VTOP:   equ 1C00h           ; variables grow down from here                   TIB:    equ 1C00h           ; command line                   NBUF:   equ 1C60h           ; 12 digits from the chip                   ABUF:   equ 1C80h           ; ASK's input line                   STK:    equ 1F00h           ; the monitor uses 1Fxx                   MAGICV: equ 0F0CAh                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- the chip                   ; Send instruction A to the MM57109, as BURP does: wait until it is ready,                   ; put the instruction on its lines, wait until it takes it, then set HOLD so                   ; it stops after it.                    ; COMP80 PILOT                   ;                   ; PILOT, the 1970s teaching language, for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM                   ; (0400h-0BFFh) that held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As                   ; with BURP, the RS key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; A line typed with a number in front is stored in the program (a number on                   ; its own deletes that line); LIST, RUN and NEW work on the program; any                   ; other line runs at once.  A statement is                   ;                   ;   [*LABEL] OP[Y|N][(CONDITION)]:TEXT                   ;                   ;   T: type TEXT, with $X and #X replaced by the variables' values                   ;   A: accept a line into the answer; A:$X or A:#X also keeps it in X                   ;   M: match: Y if any of TEXT's comma-separated words is in the answer                   ;   J: jump to a label        U: use a label as a subroutine                   ;   E: end a subroutine, or the program                   ;   C: compute: C:#X=EXPRESSION or C:$X=TEXT                   ;   G: plot point X,Y on the 128 x 62 quarter-block screen; G: alone clears                   ;   R: remark                   ;                   ; OPY and OPN only run when the last M: matched or didn't; Y: and N: are                   ; short for TY: and TN:.  (CONDITION) is an expression, or two compared with                   ; < > = <> <= >=.  Expressions are 16-bit integers with + - * / ( ), #X or X                   ; for a variable and ?N for a random number from 1 to N.                   ;                   ; Variables: #A-#Z are numbers, $A-$Z strings of up to 31 characters.                   ;                   ; Program lines are kept in order of number from PROG: number (2 bytes),                   ; length of the whole record (1), text, 0.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are as in FORTH: the monitor's NMI handler echoes each key                   ; at (DE); RS while waiting for a key is rubout; any key while a program runs                   ; resets to the monitor and RS comes back with the program kept.  Line 0                   ; shows PILOT, lines 1-31 scroll.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the program below is valid                   PEND:   equ 0C02h           ; end of the program                   SEED:   equ 0C04h           ; random number seed                   PROG:   equ 0C06h           ; first program line                   PTOP:   equ 1980h           ; the program must end below here                   MAGICV: equ 0A11Ch                    SVARS:  equ 1980h           ; $A-$Z, 32 bytes each                   ANS:    equ 1CC0h           ; the answer (80 bytes)                   TIB:    equ 1D10h           ; input line (80 bytes)                   NVARS:  equ 1D60h           ; #A-#Z, 2 bytes each                   VEND:   equ 1D94h                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   LP:     equ 1DA2h           ; line running, or 0                   NLP:    equ 1DA4h           ; line to run next; 0FFFFh to stop                   FLAG:   equ 1DA6h           ; 'Y' or 'N', set by M:                   USP:    equ 1DA8h           ; U: stack pointer                   USTK:   equ 1DAAh           ; U: stack, 8 return lines                   USTKL:  equ 0AAh            ; low bytes of USTK and of its end                   USTKE:  equ 0BAh                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; machine stack (the monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- terminal                    ; Wait for a key. ZASM

A Z80 assembler and disassembler covering every documented instruction. ASM is the disassembler run backwards: it tries each opcode until its text matches the line typed. Source: zasm/zasm.asm.

                   ; COMP80 ZASM                   ;                   ; A Z80 assembler and disassembler for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM                   ; (0400h-0BFFh) that held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As                   ; with BURP, the RS key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Commands (numbers in hex, as in the monitor; only the first letter counts):                   ;   DIS [addr]           disassemble 24 lines; with no address, carry on                   ;   ASM [addr]           assemble a line at a time; a blank line ends                   ;   GO addr              call addr; a RET comes back here                   ;                   ; Decoding follows the opcode's fields: x = bits 7-6, y = 5-3, z = 2-0, and                   ; y = p * 2 + q.  For x = 0 and x = 3 (and ED with x = 1) a table indexed by                   ; z gives a list of format strings and which field picks one from it.  A                   ; format string is text with control codes (below 20h) for the operands; its                   ; last byte has bit 7 set.                   ;                   ; The assembler runs the disassembler backwards.  It tries every opcode in                   ; turn (plain, CB, ED, DD, FD, DD CB, FD CB) in a 4-byte buffer, with the                   ; disassembler in "template" mode: instead of being printed, each character                   ; is compared with the line typed in, and the first mismatch gives up that                   ; opcode.  Where a number would be printed, the typed number is read instead                   ; and kept with the place it goes, so the first opcode whose text matches is                   ; the instruction.  Typed numbers must start with a digit (0FF, not FF), as                   ; the disassembler prints them, so that A, B, C and so on are registers.                   ; Relative jumps take the address jumped to.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are handled as in COMP80 FORTH (forth/forth.asm).                    TIB:    equ 1D00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   DPTR:   equ 1DA2h           ; next byte to disassemble                   OPTR:   equ 1DA4h           ; template mode: next character to match                   PFX:    equ 1DA6h           ; 0, DD or FD                   TMPL:   equ 1DA8h           ; nonzero: template mode                   OPY:    equ 1DA9h                   OPZ:    equ 1DAAh                   DVAL:   equ 1DABh           ; index displacement                   POSN:   equ 1DACh           ; where the number goes                   POSD:   equ 1DAEh           ; where the displacement goes                   TSP:    equ 1DB6h           ; stack pointer to give up a try                   NEXTA:  equ 1DB8h           ; where DIS carries on                   DEST:   equ 1DBAh           ; where ASM puts the next instruction                   IPTR:   equ 1DBCh           ; command line parse position                   LSTART: equ 1DBEh           ; start of the ASM line on screen                   GPTR:   equ 1DC0h           ; assembler: group being tried                   GCNT:   equ 1DC2h                   CBUF:   equ 1DC8h           ; assembler: the instruction being tried                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; stack (the monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                    ; control codes in format strings                   RY:     equ 1               ; r[y]                   RZ:     equ 2               ; r[z]                   RPP:    equ 3               ; rp[p]: BC DE HL SP                   RP2:    equ 4               ; rp2[p]: BC DE HL AF                   CCY:    equ 5               ; cc[y]                   CC4:    equ 6               ; cc[y-4]                   NB:     equ 7               ; a byte                   NW:     equ 8               ; a word                   REL:    equ 9               ; relative jump, shown as its target                   ALU:    equ 10              ; ADD A, ADC A, SUB ... CP                   ROT:    equ 11              ; RLC ... SRL                   BITY:   equ 12              ; y as a digit                   RSTY:   equ 13              ; y * 8                   IMY:    equ 14              ; interrupt mode for y                   HLX:    equ 15              ; HL, IX or IY                   BLI:    equ 16              ; block instruction                   LDS:    equ 17              ; "LD "                   E:      equ 80h             ; added to the last byte of a string                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- decoder                    ; Disassemble the instruction at DPTR: print it, or in template mode match                   ; it against the text at OPTR.                    ; COMP80 PROLOG                   ;                   ; A small Prolog for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that                   ; held BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS                   ; key enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; The keyboard and screen have no lower case, so a variable is a single                   ; letter, or a letter followed by digits (X, Y, L1); any other name is an                   ; atom.  ? is an anonymous variable, and [H:T] is a list with head H and                   ; tail T, as | and _ can't be typed.                   ;                   ; Terms are 16-bit words:                   ;   number n     2n+1 (odd), so -16384..16383                   ;   atom         address of its record in 0C30h-0EFFh: length (1), name;                   ;                records start on addresses that are multiples of 4                   ;   cell         address of a 4-byte cell, car then cdr, in the heap                   ;                (1000h up, or 8800h up with the 32 KB expansion)                   ;   variable     address of a cell + 2: the cell's car is what it is bound                   ;                to, or 0 while it is unbound                   ; A compound term f(a,b) is the list of cells (f a b ...) ending in 0, and                   ; a list [a,b] is cells (a . (b . [])) ending in the atom [].  Inside a                   ; stored clause, variable k is 4k+6 and the end of the body is 2 (the hole).                   ;                   ; A clause is the cell (head . body), the body a list of goals ending in the                   ; hole, and the database is a list of clauses.  To use a clause, the solver                   ; copies it into the heap with fresh variables, the hole replaced by the                   ; goals still to be done (the continuation) and each ! by the depth of the                   ; choice point stack to cut back to (as an odd number, so a goal that is a                   ; number is a cut).  So a goal list is just a list, ending in 0 when the                   ; query is proved.                   ;                   ; Choice points are on the Z80 stack: the continuation, the next clause to                   ; try, the trail pointer and the heap pointer.  Every binding goes on the                   ; trail, which grows down from the top of the heap.  Backtracking pops a                   ; choice point, unbinds what was bound since, and gives the heap back.                   ; Nothing is collected: the heap is cleared after each query.                   ;                   ; Text is kept in ASCII (20h-5Fh) and converted to the display's 6-bit codes                   ; on output.  Keys and the screen work as in COMP80 FORTH (forth/forth.asm):                   ; RS while waiting for a key is rubout, any key while a program runs resets                   ; to the monitor, and RS from there comes back to Prolog with the clauses                   ; kept.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the RAM below holds clauses                   SYMEND: equ 0C02h           ; end of the symbol table                   DBHEAD: equ 0C04h           ; first cell of the database, or 0: the cdr                   DBTAIL: equ 0C06h           ; of a cell at 0C02h, the last one at first                   HPERM:  equ 0C08h           ; heap top after the clauses                   HP:     equ 0C0Ah           ; heap top                   TR:     equ 0C0Ch           ; the trail: a list of the variables bound                   CURS:   equ 0C0Eh           ; output position in screen memory                   TOIN:   equ 0C10h           ; byte: read offset into TIB                   NTIB:   equ 0C11h           ; byte: characters in TIB                   NVARS:  equ 0C12h           ; byte: variables in the clause read                   HOLE:   equ 0C14h           ; what COPY puts in place of the hole                   B0:     equ 0C16h           ; what COPY puts in place of ! (less 1)                   CONT:   equ 0C18h           ; goals still to prove                   REST:   equ 0C1Ah           ; the goals after GOAL                   GOAL:   equ 0C1Ch           ; the goal being proved                   KEY:    equ 0C1Eh           ; its name                   SPSV:   equ 0C20h           ; SP with the choice points, for FAIL                   BASE:   equ 0C22h           ; SP with no choice points                   HBASE:  equ 0C24h           ; first cell        } set at cold start                   HLIM:   equ 0C26h           ; end of the heap   } from MEM8 or MEM32                   SLIM:   equ 0C28h           ; lowest SP for a new choice point                   CLS:    equ 0C2Ah           ; the clause being tried                   SYMS:   equ 0C30h           ; symbol table, up to SYMTOP                   SYMTOP: equ 0F00h                   TIB:    equ 0F00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   FRAME:  equ 0F50h           ; the 16 variables of the clause being copied                   VNAMES: equ 0F70h           ; the names of the variables read                   QVS:    equ 0F90h           ; the variables of the query                   WBUF:   equ 0FB0h           ; name being read, counted (80 bytes, so any                                               ; name on a line fits)                   STOP:   equ 1F00h           ; Z80 stack grows down from here (monitor uses 1Fxx)                   MAGICV: equ 0D16Ah                    CUTA:   equ SYMS            ; the first symbol records, 8 bytes apart                   NILA:   equ SYMS+8          ; (see NAMES)                   BUILT:  equ SYMS+16         ; the built-in predicates                   NBUILT: equ 7                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; As with BURP, the RS key enters it:                   ; the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; Every statement is an assignment, one to a line: V=E.  A space ends it, so                   ; anything after one is a comment, and a line starting ) is all comment.                   ; Numbers are 16-bit unsigned, 0-65535, and an expression is worked out from                   ; left to right with no precedence: + - * / and = < > (> is greater or                   ; equal), which give 1 or 0, and brackets.  Every printable character is a                   ; variable; some are special:                   ;   #   the line number.  #=E goes to line E (the first line from E on), or                   ;       on to the next line if E is 0; ! is set to the line after.                   ;   !   so #=! comes back from a subroutine.                   ;   ?   ?="TEXT" prints and starts a new line (not with a ; after it);                   ;       ?=E prints a number; A=? reads one, typed as an expression.                   ;   $   $=E prints the character E (13 is a new line); A=$ waits for a key.                   ;   &   the end of the program; &=0 clears it.     *   the top of memory.                   ;   '   a random number; '=E sets the seed.         %   the remainder of the                   ;       last division.                   ;   :E) an array in the memory after the program.                   ;   @   @=E plots point E, Y*128+X, on the 128 x 62 quarter-character points                   ;       of lines 1-31; adding 8192 clears it instead.                   ; A line typed with a number goes into the program (a number alone deletes                   ; it); 0 lists the program, and a line without a number runs at once: #=1                   ; runs the program.                   ;                   ; The program is kept as typed: each line its number (2 bytes, low first),                   ; its text without the leading spaces, and 0Dh.  Lines are in order from                   ; 0C04h up to TXTEND (&).  The variables are 64 words at 1C00h, one for each                   ; character from 20h to 5Fh.  Statements run straight from the text: DE is                   ; the text pointer throughout.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are handled as in COMP80 FORTH: the monitor's NMI handler                   ; echoes each key and wakes the HALT in RAWKEY; RS while waiting is a rubout                   ; and RS at any other time (re)starts VTL-2, keeping the program.  Any key                   ; while a program runs resets to the monitor; RS comes back with the                   ; program kept.  Line 0 shows VTL-2; lines 1-31 scroll.                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the program below is valid                   TXTEND: equ 0C02h           ; end of the program: &                   PROG:   equ 0C04h           ; first line                   MAGICV: equ 07714h                   TOP:    equ 1C00h           ; *: the program and :) end below here                   VARS:   equ 1C00h           ; a word for each character 20h-5Fh                   VBANG:  equ VARS+2*('!'-20h)                   VPCT:   equ VARS+2*('%'-20h)                   TIB:    equ 1D00h           ; input line (80 bytes; page aligned)                   TIB2:   equ 1E00h           ; a number typed for ? (the same)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   CURLN:  equ 1DA2h           ; the line running, 0 for a line typed in                   RNDV:   equ 1DA4h           ; random number                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; stack (monitor uses 1Fxx)                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- expressions                   ;                    ; COMP80 MOUSE                   ;                   ; Mouse, Peter Grogono's little stack language (BYTE, July 1979), for the PSI                   ; COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that held BURP.  The monitor                   ; (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS key enters it: the                   ; monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.  It is new, written from scratch.                   ;                   ; A line starting with a digit is a program line: its number orders it and                   ; a number on its own deletes it.  LIST, RUN and NEW work on the program;                   ; any other line runs at once (start it with a space if it begins with a                   ; number).  The program's lines run as one stream of text, the line numbers                   ; left out, and it ends at $ or $$; macro definitions follow.                   ;                   ;   0-9    push a number               A-Z  push a variable's address                   ;   :      store (value addr :)        .    fetch (addr .)                   ;   + - * /  arithmetic, % remainder   < = >  compare, giving 1 or 0                   ;   !      print a number              !'   print a character                   ;   !.     plot point x y (x < 0 clears the screen)                   ;   ?      read a number               ?'   read a character                   ;   ?.     random number from 1 to the number on the stack                   ;   "TEXT" print TEXT, ! in it a new line                   ;   'C     push the character C        [ .. ]  do it if the number is > 0                   ;   ( .. )  loop                       &    leave the loop if the number is <= 0                   ;   #A,P1,P2;  call macro A           $A .. @  define macro A                   ;   %1 .. %9   a macro's parameters    $ or $$  end of the program                   ;                   ; ^ (the RS key), \ and _ can't be typed on the COMP80, so the loop's                   ; ^ is & here and remainder (\) is % (when not followed by a digit).  ~                   ; can't be typed either, so there are no comments.                   ;                   ; Memory is 768 16-bit words.  A letter is address 0-25 plus OFFSET, which                   ; goes up by 26 for each macro call, so each call has its own variables;                   ; the words above those used by the calls make arrays.                   ;                   ; Frames on the control stack (IY), 8 bytes each: type ('L' loop, 'M'                   ; macro, 'P' parameter), 0, position to go back to, the macro call's                   ; position (M), OFFSET to go back to.  IX is the data stack.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are as in FORTH: the monitor's NMI handler echoes each key                   ; at (DE); RS while waiting for a key is rubout; any key while a program runs                   ; resets to the monitor and RS comes back with the program kept.  Line 0                   ; shows MOUSE, lines 1-31 scroll.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV when the program below is valid                   PEND:   equ 0C02h           ; end of the program                   SEED:   equ 0C04h           ; random number seed                   PROG:   equ 0C06h           ; first program line: number (2), length (1), text, 0                   PTOP:   equ 1400h           ; the program must end below here                   MAGICV: equ 0A0C5h                    MEM:    equ 1400h           ; 768 words                   MEMW:   equ 768                   DSTK:   equ 1A00h           ; data stack, 64 words (page aligned)                   ESTK0:  equ 1A80h           ; a frame of type 0 below the control stack                   ESTK:   equ 1A88h           ; control stack frames                   ESTKE:  equ 1D00h                   TIB:    equ 1D10h           ; input line (80 bytes)                   ANS:    equ 1D60h           ; line read by ? (32 bytes)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   POS:    equ 1DA2h           ; next character of the program to run                   OFFSET: equ 1DA4h           ; variables of the macro call running                   DEFS:   equ 1DB0h           ; where each macro's text starts, 26 words                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; machine stack (the monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   CLS64:  equ 0393h           ; monitor: spaces from 8040h to the end of the screen                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ; monitor: spaces at (DE) up to the next line                            org 0400h                    ; ---------------------------------------------------------------- terminal                    ; Wait for a key. Befunge

Befunge-93 with the screen as its playfield, so programs that change themselves change in front of you. Source: befunge/befunge.asm.

                   ; COMP80 BEFUNGE                   ;                   ; Befunge-93 for the PSI COMP80, in the 2 KB of ROM (0400h-0BFFh) that held                   ; BURP.  The monitor (0000h-03FFh) is unchanged.  As with BURP, the RS key                   ; enters it: the monitor's NMI handler jumps to 0800h.                   ;                   ; The program is the screen: lines 1-24 are the 64 x 24 playfield, which                   ; wraps round at its edges, and the instruction pointer runs over the                   ; characters you can see.  G and P read and write those same characters, so                   ; a program that changes itself changes on the screen.  Line 0 shows BEFUNGE                   ; and, after STEP, where the pointer is and the top of the stack; lines 25-31                   ; are for commands and the program's output, and scroll by themselves.                   ;                   ; Commands:                   ;   Y X TEXT   put TEXT on line Y (0-23) of the playfield from column X                   ;              (0-63); exactly one space after X, then TEXT as it stands                   ;   EDIT Y X   type straight onto the playfield from there: Return goes to                   ;              the next line, RS steps back, Return on a line where nothing                   ;              has been typed ends                   ;   RUN        run from the top left corner, going right, with an empty stack                   ;   STEP       do one instruction, show the pointer and the stack                   ;   SPEED N    wait N (0-255) between instructions, showing the pointer as a                   ;              block; 0 runs flat out                   ;   CLEAR      blank the playfield                   ;                   ; The keyboard can't type ^ _ or \, and the screen has no | ` or ~, so:                   ;   type '  for ^ (up)       = for _ (horizontal if)     ; for \ (swap)                   ;   I is | (vertical if),  ) is ` (greater than),  ( is ~ (read a character)                   ;   and G P V are g p v.  ' = and ; are turned into ^ _ and \ as they are                   ;   typed, in strings too.                   ;                   ; Cells hold a byte.  A cell's value is its character's ASCII code: the                   ; screen codes 00h-1Fh (@ A-Z [ \ ] ^ _) are ASCII 40h-5Fh and 20h-3Fh are                   ; themselves; the other values, 00h-1Fh and 60h-FFh, show as graphics.                   ; Numbers on the stack are 16-bit.  Division by 0 gives 0.                   ;                   ; Keys and screen are as in FORTH: the monitor's NMI handler echoes each key                   ; at (DE); RS while waiting for a key is rubout; any key while a program runs                   ; resets to the monitor, and RS comes back with the playfield kept.                    MAGIC:  equ 0C00h           ; MAGICV once set up                   IPX:    equ 0C02h           ; pointer column                   IPY:    equ 0C03h           ; pointer line                   DX:     equ 0C04h           ; direction across: 1, 0 or -1                   DY:     equ 0C05h           ; direction down                   STRM:   equ 0C06h           ; not 0 in string mode                   HALTED: equ 0C07h           ; not 0 once the program has ended                   SPEED:  equ 0C08h                   SEED:   equ 0C0Ah           ; random number seed                   BSP:    equ 0C0Ch           ; Befunge stack pointer                   MARKA:  equ 0C0Eh           ; cell showing the pointer, or 0                   MARKC:  equ 0C10h           ; what is really in it                   EDX:    equ 0C11h           ; EDIT: column, line, first column,                   EDY:    equ 0C12h           ;   and whether anything was typed on the line                   EDX0:   equ 0C13h                   EDN:    equ 0C14h                   TCURS:  equ 0C16h           ; the text cursor while editing                   STK0:   equ 0C20h           ; Befunge stack, up to 1C00h                   STKEH:  equ 1Ch                   MAGICV: equ 0BEF9h                    TIB:    equ 1D00h           ; input line (80 bytes)                   CURS:   equ 1DA0h           ; output position in screen memory                   S0:     equ 1F00h           ; machine stack (the monitor uses 1Fxx)                    VRAM:   equ 8000h                   GRID:   equ 8040h           ; the playfield, lines 1-24                   TEXT:   equ 8640h           ; lines 25-31                   MARK:   equ 4Fh             ; a solid block shows the pointer                   PAD64:  equ 03C4h           ;
